blocks.text: In Leo Africanus, Descript. Africae book 9, ch. 53, this lizard is called Guaral. An animal, he says, similar to the aforementioned [Dub, ضبّ [ḍabb]] but somewhat larger; it likewise carries venom in its head and tail, and when these parts have been cut off the Arabs are accustomed to eat it; otherwise it is ugly and of a foul colour. But ورل [waral] must not be confused with وَرَنٌ [waranun], which in Giggeius is rendered a species of reptile, but which, on Forskål's testimony, is the name of the Nile lizard; see Descriptiones Animalium, quae in itinere Orientali observavit Petrus Forskal, p. 13.

But Michaelis rightly points out in the Supplemm. vol. 4, p. 1221, that several further etymologies present themselves, not considered by Bochart, to which the name of that lizard could be referred. We have already noted quite often that this method, fishing out the meanings of the names that denote animals by etymologies alone, is wholly uncertain. The name כח seems to be one of those whose meaning we must utterly despair of determining, since we lack the aid both of the other dialects and of passages from which the nature and character of this animal might be known well enough for anything certain to be established about it.
